messages.author: dde40b6e9b2ec6e4
messages.subject: Doubt about inla.spde2.pcmatern and inla.spde2.matern
parts:
Dear INLA Community

I am trying to compare the difference between spde2.pcmatern and spde2.matern, I know that one of them, spde2.pcmatern allows to obtain the range and variance meanwhile spde2.materns returns kappa and tau, but doing this I was left with some questions:

1-. Is there any way to transform kappa and tau into range and variance to compare how much they change because of the prior selection?

2-. I also see that the precision for the observation changes but I thought that inla.spde2.pcmatern was only for the hyperparameters so I am not really sure why this value changes

3-. Is there any way to know the prior selected by spde2.matern because as long as I understand this is selected because of the mesh but I am not sure if there is any way to check which one was selected?

Thank you

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Doubt about inla.spde2.pcmatern and inla.spde2.matern
parts:
Hi,
The inla.spde.result() function can be used to convert to range and variance for inla.spde2.matern models. You can also use inla.tmarginal and related functions directly (e.g. to transform to standard deviation)

The prior is part of the model, so priors for one parameter will affect the estimation of other parameters.

When inla.spde2.matern, you should really specify the parameters for the priors. We discuss how to do that in the 2015 https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19 paper.
Using the default values is not recommended.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Doubt about inla.spde2.pcmatern and inla.spde2.matern
parts:
Hi,

you can transform the quantiles like that, yes. The posterior mean and
standard deviation are more involved. However, you can look at the
code to see how the transformation is done.
Also, inla.spde.posterior by default should give you the range and
variance posteriors directly, not just log(range) and log(variance).

The "precision for the lognormal observations" is the precision
parameter of the observation model. See INLA::inla.doc("lognormal")
for the exact definition of the model.

"nugget effect" is just a shorthand name for "random independent
additive noise" when applied to covariance models, and isn't
necessarily a useful term in general, but yes, the observation noise
can be seen as a "nugget effect".
Terminology-wise, I'd say that the "nugget effect" _has_ a variance
(and variance is the inverse of precision), not that it _is_ variance.
But the precision parameter of a _lognormal_ distribution is not the
inverse of the precision of the lognormal variable, unless one uses a
parameterisation that makes that true; it's more common that it's the
precision of the logarithm of the lognormal variable. See the
inla.doc() document for the actual definition in the INLA model
context.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Doubt about inla.spde2.pcmatern and inla.spde2.matern
parts:
﻿Hi,
No, you don’t need kappa; each SPDE model object has its own parameterisation, so the one for spde2.matern is not the same as for spde2.pcmatern.

Usually you can get posterior samples from inla,posterior.sample (or generate()/oredict() when using inlabru) which handles this automatically.
But if you want unconditional samples, you can use inla.spde.precision() followed by inla.qsample(). The first function takes the log of the 2-parameter vector as input,
which is either log(c(range, sigma)) or log(c(sigma, range)) when using the pcmatern model. Try different values to find out the correct order…

Finn

you can transform the quantiles like that, yes. The posterior mean and
standard deviation are more involved. However, you can look at the
code to see how the transformation is done.
Also, inla.spde.posterior by default should give you the range and
variance posteriors directly, not just log(range) and log(variance).

The "precision for the lognormal observations" is the precision
parameter of the observation model. See INLA::inla.doc("lognormal")
for the exact definition of the model.

"nugget effect" is just a shorthand name for "random independent
additive noise" when applied to covariance models, and isn't
necessarily a useful term in general, but yes, the observation noise
can be seen as a "nugget effect".
Terminology-wise, I'd say that the "nugget effect" _has_ a variance
(and variance is the inverse of precision), not that it _is_ variance.
But the precision parameter of a _lognormal_ distribution is not the
inverse of the precision of the lognormal variable, unless one uses a
parameterisation that makes that true; it's more common that it's the
precision of the logarithm of the lognormal variable. See the
inla.doc() document for the actual definition in the INLA model
context.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Doubt about inla.spde2.pcmatern and inla.spde2.matern
parts:
Hi,

for pcmatern, the hyperparameter output already contains the range and
std.dev. parameter posterior summaries, so inla.spde2.result() doesn't
provide much additional benefits (and if you do use it, note that is
by default has nominal.range and nominal.variance in the output, not
just log of range and variance).

For transforming precision to variance, be mindful of the fact that
expectations are not invariant under transformations, but quantiles
are; i.e. you can transform the quantiles as 0.5quant_variance =
1/0.5quant_precision
and 0.95quant_variance = 1/0.05quant_precision (your expression uses
an additional square, which is incorrect; precision is 1/variance, not
1/std.dev.).
But expectations do not transform like that; E(f(X)) != f(E(X)). To
get the posterior expectation of the variance you'd need to use e.g.
rr_variance_posterior_mean = inla.emarginal(function(x) 1/x,
result$marginals.hyperpar[["Precision for rr"]])

Finally, whether the variance of rr is interpretable as "the" nugget
depends on what's in your rr variable, so it's impossible to tell just
from the code. Also, if it does give a separate value for each
observation, it depends on the observation model as well; having both
an iid component and a Gaussian observation model, e.g. is too much.

Finn

parts:
Thank you for your detailed explanation, it helped clarify a lot.

I wanted to give a bit more context on how I defined rr in my model. Essentially, rr represents the identifiers for the schools where data was collected (my geographical region points). Here's the relevant part of my code:

```
stk.e1 <- inla.stack(
  tag = 'point',
  data = list(y = dm$n, numtrials = dm$N),
  A = list(A, 1, 1),
  effects = list(
    s = indexs,
    rr = 1:length(dm$elevation_cat),
    data.frame(
      b0 = 1,
      x1 = dm2$elevation,
      x3 = dm2$open_def_cat,
      x2 = dm2$prec_cat
    )
  )
)
mod <- inla(
  formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = numtrials,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
  control.family = control.family(link = 'logit'),
  control.predictor = list(
    compute = TRUE,
    link = 1,
    A = inla.stack.A(stk.full)
  ),
  control.compute = list(config = TRUE, return.marginals.predictor = TRUE, cpo = T),
  control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-7),
  num.threads = 7,
  verbose = F
)

```
Finally, my observational model is based on a binomial distribution where y is the number of successes (positive cases) and N is the total number of trials (children tested).
